source: Ritchey (2002, rev. 2013) General Morphological Analysis: a general method for non-quantified modelling
finding: Zwicky built morphological analysis at Caltech from the 1940s to 1974. A morphological box (Zwicky box) sets parameters against each other. Each cell holds one value per parameter and marks one configuration.
numbers: Toy box: 5x5x3 = 75 cells. Zwicky applied it to astrophysical object classes, jet and rocket propulsion, and space law.
quote: Each cell of the n-dimensional box contains one particular 'value' or condition from each of the parameters
limits: Secondary source by Zwicky's main modern successor. Ritchey is an advocate, not a neutral tester.
agent_relevance: S3 open mode: the box is a plain data structure (parameters x values) that code can hold and enumerate exactly.

source: Ritchey (2002, rev. 2013) General Morphological Analysis: a general method for non-quantified modelling
finding: Cross-consistency assessment (CCA) is Zwicky's 'principle of contradiction and reduction'. Every pair of values is judged for mutual consistency, with no causal direction. Configurations with any incompatible pair are dropped.
numbers: Configurations grow exponentially, pair judgments grow quadratically. A field with about 100,000 configurations needs only a few hundred pair judgments. Shelter study: 6-parameter segment (4x4x4x3x3x4) = 2304 configs, 15 pair relations marked; full 10-parameter field > 500,000 configs.
limits: Pair-only checking assumes conflicts are pairwise. Triple-wise conflicts are missed. Judgments are human opinion.
agent_relevance: Strong fit for the schema: model supplies cheap pairwise judgments, code does the combinatorial filtering. Pair count is quadratic, so a call budget can be planned in advance.

source: Ritchey (2002, rev. 2013) General Morphological Analysis: a general method for non-quantified modelling
finding: Three kinds of inconsistency: logical contradiction, empirical implausibility, normative constraint. Normative judgments are kept out of the first CCA pass so that 'what is possible' is separated from 'what is desirable'.
numbers: Same Swedish shelter study (Swedish National Rescue Agency).
quote: we only allow logical and empirical judgements to be made initially
limits: Normative filtering later is still human judgment.
agent_relevance: Staged filtering: logic and empirical first, preferences second. Matches G3 (check on something the answer was not fitted to) and keeps taste out of feasibility.

source: Ritchey (2002, rev. 2013) General Morphological Analysis: a general method for non-quantified modelling
finding: Claimed benefits: a traceable audit trail, 'garbage detection' because vague parameter definitions fail at the CCA step, and good group work. Identical fields given to different groups for CCA gave diverging assessments, which were used to find real disagreements.
numbers: More than 100 computer-aided GMA projects since 1995 (Swedish Defence Research Agency). No agreement statistic given.
limits: No inter-rater numbers. Self-reported by the method's developer.
agent_relevance: Fields and pair judgments are loggable artifacts. Disagreement between samples is itself a signal, in line with G1 (doubt on a signal).

source: Ritchey (2006) Problem structuring using computer-aided morphological analysis, JORS 57
finding: History: Zwicky jet engines 1947, morphological astronomy 1948, method paper 1948, book 1966/1969. Norris (1963) proposed it as an engineering design method with computers. Rhyne (1971, 1981, SRI) used a restricted form for scenarios under the name field anomaly relaxation.
numbers: Ritchey's own count: GMA 'has been written about and discussed far more than it has actually been used in real client-based projects'.
quote: None of this seems to have had much of an impact on OR-techniques or PSMs generally.
limits: Ritchey blames manual effort for low use; he is not a neutral judge.
agent_relevance: Warns that the method's literature is mostly case reports, not tests. The agent should not assume proven benefit.

source: Ritchey (2006) Problem structuring using computer-aided morphological analysis, JORS 57
finding: Zwicky's propulsive-system morphology (dated 1947 here) has 6 parameters and 576 formal configurations. Typical modern fields have 6-10 parameters with 50,000 to 5,000,000 configurations, too many to inspect by hand. CCA is said to cut a field by 90 to 99 percent.
numbers: 576 = 4x4x3x3x2x2. Reduction claim: 90-99 percent depending on structure (scenario fields are an exception).
limits: Reduction rate is a claim, not measured across projects. The date for the 576 field differs between Ritchey papers (1947 here, 1962 in the 2015 survey).
agent_relevance: A mid-size field is far beyond a model's context but trivial for code. Argues for code enumeration with model-judged pair compatibility.

source: Ritchey (2006) Problem structuring using computer-aided morphological analysis, JORS 57
finding: Worked case: Swedish extended producer responsibility (EPR) system. Scenario field had 8 parameters and 20,736 configurations; 8 were chosen to cover every parameter state. Strategy field had 8 parameters and 34,560 configurations, reduced by CCA to 480.
numbers: 34,560 to 480 = 98.6 percent removed. Linking both fields would give over 700 million configurations, so the scenario was merged in as one placeholder parameter instead.
limits: Single project, no outcome measure of decision quality.
agent_relevance: Real reduction ratio from a deployed use. Also shows the cure for explosion: collapse a sub-field into one placeholder parameter, then link.

source: Ritchey (2006) Problem structuring using computer-aided morphological analysis, JORS 57
finding: Two ways to assess a linked scenario parameter: a quick method (scenario as a whole against each strategy parameter) and a thorough method. The quick method is used when group time is short.
numbers: No timing data reported.
limits: Quick method skips the scenario's internal states.
agent_relevance: A cheap and a thorough tier for a budgeted agent.

source: Ritchey (1998) Fritz Zwicky, Morphologie and Policy Analysis
finding: Zwicky's five iterative steps (from his book): formulate the problem concisely; localise and analyse all relevant parameters; build the morphological box of all potential solutions; scrutinise and evaluate each solution against the purpose; select and apply the best, which needs a further morphological study.
numbers: Five steps. Zwicky used 40 or more dimensions in some studies.
quote: The problem to be solved must be very concisely formulated.
limits: Steps as summarised by Ritchey, not read in the 1969 book.
agent_relevance: Maps onto states: frame (step 1), parameter listing (2), enumerate (3), evaluate (4), select (5). Parameter choice is the hard model step; steps 3 and 4 can be code plus checks.

source: Ritchey (1998) Fritz Zwicky, Morphologie and Policy Analysis
finding: Zwicky called the method 'totality research': derive all solutions, unbiased. He saw complete field coverage as a way to push thinking to the limits of the conceivable, not as a brake on creativity. Ritchey rebuts the objection that the method is too rigid.
numbers: No empirical test cited for the creativity claim.
quote: For him, the whole point of morphological analysis and systematic complete field coverage is to push consciousness to the limits of the conceivable
limits: The claim that structure does not hurt creativity is asserted, not measured.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema idea of forced coverage of a space, but see a14 and a16 to a18 for the human cost and the thin test base.

source: Ritchey (1998) Fritz Zwicky, Morphologie and Policy Analysis
finding: Zwicky's own example: match 10 energy forms against themselves in a 2-dimensional table to list every conversion. Ritchey extends it to 3 steps with 5 forms. Biography: Caltech faculty 1927-68, Aerojet research director 1943-61, co-founder of Aerojet, led US teams evaluating German and Japanese jet research after WWII.
numbers: 2-dim: 10x10 cells. 3-step with 5 forms: 5^3 = 125 configurations.
limits: Biographical detail from a short appreciation by Ritchey.
agent_relevance: Pairwise 'forms against forms' tables are an easy operator: one cell, one judgment.

source: Alvarez and Ritchey (2015) Applications of General Morphological Analysis, Acta Morphologica Generalis 4(1)
finding: Survey of roughly 80 published GMA applications, from engineering design to policy. Describes Zwicky's telescope example from Morphological Astronomy (1948): N = nA x nB x nC ... Zwicky stresses two superimposed tasks: discard impossible combinations, and stay open to strange new ones.
numbers: 6 parameters of 4 values each give 4096 combinations. Propulsive power morphology: 6 dimensions, 576 (4x4x3x3x2x2) configurations, dated 1962 here.
quote: two strangely superimposed (and what might seem to be mentally contradictory) tasks
limits: A bibliography of reports, not a test of effect. Selection of papers is by the authors.
agent_relevance: Gives the counting rule for code. Names the dual task (prune and stay open), which the schema should keep apart.

source: Alvarez and Ritchey (2015) Applications of General Morphological Analysis, Acta Morphologica Generalis 4(1)
finding: Engineering-design applications cited: Norris 1963, Weber and Condor 1989 (synergistically compatible matrix), Evbuomwan 1997, Dartnall and Johnston 2005, Jimenez and Mavris 2010 (systems engineering), Zeiler 2009 and 2011 (architecture). Given with abstracts only.
numbers: About 80 articles. No effect sizes.
limits: Abstract-level coverage.
agent_relevance: Source list for angle B and C searches. The design literature is application-heavy and test-light.

source: Oppenlaender (2021) Morphological Matrices as a Tool for Crowdsourced Ideation (arXiv 2110.04129)
finding: Pilot: MTurk workers asked to design a persuasive product open-ended; every submission was unusable. Feasibility test: give workers a pre-made morphological matrix and ask them to pick one option per row and describe the product. The author reports significantly more valid ideas with the matrix.
numbers: Pilot: 12 workers, 12 of 12 (100 percent) rejected. Feasibility: 12 submitted, 5 (41.67 percent) rejected, 7 effortful, only 4 gave a valid idea. No test statistic given.
quote: valid and significantly more relevant ideas
limits: Work-in-progress, tiny N, no control arm in the same design, 'significantly' is not backed by a test. Matrix options were curated from an earlier design journey, so the creative step was done by the author.
agent_relevance: A pre-filled box lowers effort but also lowers the creative leap. The agent's value is in building the parameters and values, not in picking from a given box.

source: Oppenlaender (2021) Morphological Matrices as a Tool for Crowdsourced Ideation (arXiv 2110.04129)
finding: Proposes a three-step crowd procedure: workers first generate sub-problems, then define functions, then fill options. Notes that the function structure 'depends on the solutions that are considered' and vice versa.
numbers: Proposal only, not tested.
limits: Cites Fiorineschi et al. 2016 for the circularity.
agent_relevance: Parameter choice and value choice are coupled. One pass of 'list parameters then list values' can be wrong; allow a revision when a pair check fails.

source: Hu, Shealy, Milovanovic, Gero (2020) Concept generation techniques change patterns of brain activation during engineering design, Design Science
finding: fNIRS study of 30 engineering graduate students using brainstorming, morphological analysis and TRIZ, each on a different task. Morphological analysis drove significantly more prefrontal activation than TRIZ and more than brainstorming. It was also slower than brainstorming.
numbers: N=30 (3 dropped for weak signal). Overall activation F(2,57)=29.5, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.509. TRIZ lower than brainstorming t=4.68 and lower than morphological analysis t=7.62 (both p<0.001). Morphological > brainstorming t=2.94, p=0.013. Mean time: brainstorming 7.53 min (SD 3.25), morphological 11.02 (SD 4.70), TRIZ 13.34 (SD 5.03).
limits: Only the idea-generation step was analysed per technique. Different task per technique. Brief training, no prior experience. Brain activation is a proxy for load, not for quality; no idea-quality outcome.
agent_relevance: In humans the method costs more working-memory effort than a rule-based one. Offloading enumeration to code removes the heaviest part for the model too.

source: Hu, Shealy, Milovanovic, Gero (2020) Concept generation techniques change patterns of brain activation during engineering design, Design Science
finding: Morphological analysis and TRIZ both raised coordination between prefrontal regions compared with brainstorming. Morphological analysis and brainstorming both loaded right lateral prefrontal cortex (linked to divergent thinking). Morphological analysis showed two activation peaks mid-process, near ventiles 6 and 12.
numbers: Network density F(2,57)=8.86, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.237. Brainstorming lower than morphological analysis (t=-2.71, p=0.013 at threshold 0.7). Morphological versus TRIZ not different.
limits: Divergent versus convergent readings of regions are reverse inference by the authors.
agent_relevance: Structure raises coordination without reducing load. Explains why forced decomposition feels helpful but is still demanding.

source: Hu, Shealy, Milovanovic, Gero (2020) Concept generation techniques change patterns of brain activation during engineering design, Design Science
finding: Authors explain morphological load: each step needs intuitive thinking because no engineering principles or catalogue guide the choice of sub-solutions. Students decomposed by function, which made association easier than free brainstorming in the medial PFC.
numbers: Medial PFC: F(2,57)=20.7, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.420; brainstorming and morphological both higher than TRIZ.
limits: Post-hoc explanation, not tested.
agent_relevance: Without a catalogue of values for a parameter, the value-listing step is where cost and error sit. A retrieved catalogue (TRIZ-like) would help.

source: Gero, Jiang, Williams (2012) Does using different concept generation techniques change the design cognition of design students? (DETC2012-71165)
finding: Protocol study: 22 mechanical engineering students taught brainstorming, morphological analysis and TRIZ, then worked in teams of two on three tasks for 45 minutes each. Coded with the function-behaviour-structure scheme. Abstract reports statistically significant differences in design cognition between techniques.
numbers: 22 students, teams of 2, 3 tasks, 45 min each. Abstract gives no effect sizes.
limits: Abstract only. Preliminary results. Process measure, not outcome quality.
agent_relevance: Techniques change process but not necessarily result quality; test the outcome, not the process.

source: Kannengiesser, Williams, Gero (2013) What do the concept generation techniques of TRIZ, morphological analysis and brainstorming have in common? (ICED13)
finding: Reported second-hand (in Alvarez and Ritchey 2015) as protocol studies with mechanical engineering students that found commonalities across the three techniques.
numbers: No numbers available.
limits: Second-hand abstract only.
agent_relevance: Suggests the techniques share a core: decompose, associate, recombine.

source: Shah, Kulkarni, Vargas-Hernandez (2000) Evaluation of idea generation methods for conceptual design: effectiveness metrics and design of experiments, J Mech Des 122
finding: Proposes outcome metrics for idea generation methods: quantity, quality, novelty, variety. Gives a direct method (whole method) and an indirect method (test components of a method). The standard yardstick for any test of a morphological method.
numbers: Four metrics, two experimental designs.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: The yardstick for any test of an S3 morphological operator. Variety is the one the box is meant to raise.

source: Eftekhari (2021) Assessment of ideation effectiveness in design thinking: the impact of morphological analysis in creative problem solving, DRS LxD
finding: Title indicates a test of morphological analysis in ideation. Full text and results could not be retrieved this session.
numbers: unknown
limits: Not read. A lead only.
agent_relevance: Follow up in angle B or C.

source: Savchenko (2020) New approach for processing cross-consistency matrix in modified morphological analysis method (IEEE SAIC)
finding: A computational variant of the cross-consistency matrix step. Only title and venue were seen.
numbers: unknown
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Lead for formal handling of the consistency matrix.

source: Ritchey (2012) Outline for a Morphology of Modelling Methods, Acta Morphologica Generalis 1(1)
finding: Ritchey uses GMA on itself. Five modelling properties span a field of 64 types (2x2x2x2x4). CCA removes types that cannot exist. 8 main types are described and 34 more are listed in a table. He did the CCA alone and says this is not how the method should be run.
numbers: 64 configurations; 8 main modelling types plus 34 listed.
quote: Out of necessity, I carried out this CCA solo. This is not the way it should be.
limits: Solo CCA by the author, no reliability check.
agent_relevance: Honest admission that a solo CCA is weak. For an agent: separate samples should do the pair judgments, and disagreement should be logged.

source: Ritchey (2022) Morphospaces: a catalogue of 52 morphological models from selected projects 1995-2017
finding: Catalogue of 52 field models from client projects (shelter policy 1995, economic crime 1998, energy sabotage 2002, global energy scenarios 2005, threat perception 2013, cascading events 2014-15, and others). Mostly scenario and policy fields, not engineering design.
numbers: 52 models over 22 years; EU 7th Framework and Swedish government clients.
limits: Models shown; no later check of whether the scenarios came true.
agent_relevance: Real fields are mostly scenario and policy work. Engineering-design evidence is thinner than the policy case reports.

source: Wikipedia (2025) Morphological analysis (problem-solving)
finding: Summary: Zwicky (Caltech) developed it for jet and rocket propulsion and astronomy. CCA removes illogical combinations. The method works backward from desired output to internals. Applications: engineering design, technology forecasting, organisational design, policy.
numbers: Bread example: six categories of four options. Page last edited 23 May 2025.
limits: Tertiary source. No critiques section.
agent_relevance: A pointer only; not used for claims.

source: McIntosh (2026) Linking generative AI and morphological analysis to conduct foresight evaluation, Foresight
finding: Uses ChatGPT 4o to score a 1976 Hudson Institute report whose scenarios were built with morphological analysis (four views of the future crossed with ten issues) against the present world. The second-most-pessimistic view fit best.
numbers: Best view fit 88 percent, most optimistic worst at 40 percent. One model, one report.
limits: Abstract only. Fit scores are the model's own judgments with no human check in the abstract. The LLM reads a box; it does not build one.
agent_relevance: An LLM filled a morphological grid cell by cell, a tolerable model task; the fit scores still need an outside check (G2, G5).

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2023) Conceptual design generation using large language models (arXiv 2306.01779)
finding: Not morphological, but the nearest measured LLM ideation baseline. GPT-3 gave 100 solutions to each of 12 design problems and was compared with crowd solutions. Experts rated LLM solutions higher on feasibility and usefulness and the crowd higher on novelty. GPT-3 repeats itself semantically over long lists. Few-shot prompts made output closer to the crowd.
numbers: 12 design problems; 600 solutions rated by 2 experts (anchored 0-2 scales). Convex hull volume: crowd 0.294 (SD 0.03); GPT-3 zero-shot novel-adjective prompt 0.186 (SD 0.07); few-shot 0.2 (SD 0.04); best LLM prompt 0.266 (SD 0.1).
limits: GPT-3 only. Rater agreement fair to moderate. Convex hull volume is sensitive to near-duplicates.
agent_relevance: Free LLM listing collapses into near-duplicates, the failure a forced-coverage box is meant to remove. Test whether a box raises hull volume.

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2023) Conceptual design generation using large language models (arXiv 2306.01779)
finding: The authors say the LLM's lower novelty comes from repetition after a few outputs and from lower variance than crowd workers.
numbers: Same study.
limits: Single-model generation.
agent_relevance: Supports code-enforced coverage (distinct values per parameter) instead of asking the model for more of the same.

source: Synthesis note: Oppenlaender 2021; Shah 2000; Hu 2020; Ritchey papers
finding: Gap check: across all sources read, no controlled experiment shows a morphological box raises idea quality over free ideation with an effect size. Evidence is case reports (about 80 in the 2015 survey, 52 catalogued fields), one pilot (N=12), and neuro and process studies. No LLM study was found that builds or enumerates a box and measures a result.
numbers: None found. arXiv API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited and the web search budget was spent, so coverage is partial.
limits: Absence under limited search. Angles B and C should search again.
agent_relevance: Treat the box as a plausible [D] design choice, not an [E] one. Measure it before trusting it.
